periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Who Is a Scientist? Activating Prior Knowledge

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.233): paired word-web on qualities of a scientist.
Let us read (p.233): sharing what students know about women scientists pictured.

time_bands.activity: Open with a brief whole-class exchange: ask students to name one word they associate with the word 'scientist.' Collect responses on the board to seed the word web.
Students work in pairs to complete the word web of qualities they associate with a scientist (Let us read, p.233). Pairs share with the class and the teacher builds a consolidated web on the board.
Display or refer students to the pictures of women scientists in the textbook (p.233). In pairs, students discuss what they know about each and share one observation aloud.
Teacher reads aloud the opening two paragraphs of the Bibha Chowdhuri profile (p.232–233) while students follow in their textbooks, pausing at unfamiliar names or places for brief clarification.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the profile of Bibha Chowdhuri, India's first woman physicist; students arrive with no assumed prior exposure, so the word-web and image discussion are the entry points, not a warm-up to prior class work. Watch for students who conflate 'scientist' with stereotypically male traits — the word-web conversation is an opportunity to surface and gently challenge those assumptions. The task of discussing women scientists in the pictures (p.233) may be left as an optional home exploration for students who wish to research further.
materials: Board or chart paper for word web

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Reading the Profile: From Kolkata to Manchester

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.237): arrange key events of Bibha's life in chronological order.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.238): answer 'Why is Bibha Chowdhuri considered a pioneer?'

time_bands.activity: Teacher and students share the reading of the main profile (p.234–237) in an unhurried read-aloud, with students taking turns paragraph by paragraph. Teacher pauses at key moments — the Bose Institute admission, the move to Manchester, the Nobel nomination — to clarify context.
Students individually sequence the six events from Bibha Chowdhuri's life listed in the 'Let us discuss' activity (p.237), then compare with a partner and resolve any differences through the text.
Whole-class check of the chronological order; teacher draws out why each event is significant, linking the sequence to the arc of Bibha's career from Kolkata to TIFR to Ahmedabad.

periods.teacher_notes: Having introduced Bibha Chowdhuri and the qualities associated with scientists, this unit moves into a sustained shared reading of the profile itself. Students sometimes confuse the sequence of institutions (Bose Institute → Manchester → TIFR → Ahmedabad → Saha Institute); the chronological ordering task directly addresses this. The homework question on pioneering (p.238) asks students to consolidate what they read today and is suited to individual written reflection.

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Unpacking the Extracts: Press Headlines and Legacy

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.237–238): read Extract 1 and answer all four sub-questions.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.238): read Extract 2 and write answers to all four sub-questions.

time_bands.activity: Brief recall of Bibha Chowdhuri's journey from Kolkata to Manchester, drawing on the chronological sequence students worked on during the shared reading of the profile, to orient the class to the extract's context.
Students read Extract 1 (p.237) silently, then the teacher reads it aloud once more, pausing at 'celebrated Nobel Laureate' and 'She has an eye for Cosmic Rays' for initial reactions.

Teacher leads a critical-reading discussion of the four sub-questions for Extract 1 (p.237–238): the significance of Blackett's Nobel status, inferences about public perception of women scientists in the 1940s, the meaning of 'celebrated', and the idiomatic phrase 'eye for'. Students jot short answers individually before sharing.
Teacher previews Extract 2 (p.238) by reading its opening two sentences aloud and asking students to predict its key argument; this sets up the homework reading independently.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the full profile in a shared-reading arc, students now engage in close critical analysis of Extract 1 from the 'Let us think and reflect' section. A common difficulty at this stage is treating the press headline 'India's New Woman Scientist' as straightforwardly celebratory; guide students to read it as a marker of novelty and gentle social surprise rather than full acceptance. Extract 2's sub-questions (p.238) are assigned for home reading since the extract continues the critical arc and benefits from unhurried individual attention.

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Deep Questions and AI on the Airwaves

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.238–239): discuss 'What does Schrödinger's nomination tell us about Bibha's abilities?'
Let us listen (p.244): listen to AI podcast and select correct options for all five questions.

time_bands.activity: Whole-class discussion of the question 'What does Bibha Chowdhuri's nomination by Erwin Schrödinger tell us about her abilities?' (p.238), building on the critical analysis of the two extracts from the profile. Students share views and the teacher draws out the significance of a Nobel scientist endorsing a woman researcher in 1950.
Teacher introduces the Tech Talks podcast about artificial intelligence, briefly framing the four segments students will hear: healthcare, sustainability, education, and accessibility.
Teacher reads the transcript of the AI podcast aloud (p.251–252) at a measured pace while students follow along and answer the five multiple-choice listening questions (p.244) in their notebooks.

Whole-class verification of answers to the five listening questions; teacher draws a brief link between the AI podcast's theme of technology benefiting humankind and the chapter's broader theme of science as a force for progress.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit pairs a comprehension discussion on Bibha's Nobel nomination with the listening task on AI — both are grounded in the theme of science and its human impact. The Schrödinger nomination question (p.238) is the most inference-demanding of the 'Let us think and reflect' set; students often describe it as an honour without unpacking what it signals about gender and scientific recognition in 1950. For the listening task, if students struggle with any option, re-read the relevant segment of the transcript rather than moving on.

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Panel Discussion: Mobile Phones — Benefit or Harm?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.244–245): five-member panel discussion on the impact of mobile phones.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the panel-discussion format and assigns roles — Moderator, Principal (opposed), Teacher (partially in favour), Parent (opposed), Student (in favour) — using the cue cards on p.244–245. Groups of five are formed.
Groups read their role cues silently and spend a quick preparation phase noting two or three points they will raise from their assigned perspective.
Each group conducts its panel discussion; the teacher circulates, coaching the Moderator to manage turn-taking and prompting quieter participants to contribute at least one point.
Two or three groups share their most compelling argument with the whole class; teacher draws brief feedback on how well each panel stayed in role and built on what the previous speaker said.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the chapter's theme of technology and human agency, moving from reading and listening to structured oral production. Students assigned the 'opposed' roles sometimes struggle to argue positions they personally disagree with; remind them that a panel discussion rehearses perspective-taking, not personal belief. Ensure the Moderator role is distributed to different students across groups so no single student monopolises the high-visibility position.

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Writing a Science Exhibition Report for the School Magazine

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.245–246): plan and draft a magazine report on the Zonal Science Exhibition.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the report format on the board: headline, reporter's name, three-paragraph structure. Using the cues on p.245–246, teacher writes one model sentence in past tense and passive voice as a class anchor.
Students plan their report individually — noting their headline, key cue points for each paragraph, and the Chief Guest's observations — before writing begins.

Students draft all three paragraphs of their report, working independently. Teacher circulates, giving brief oral guidance on passive construction and third-person register to students who request it.

Students exchange reports with a partner and check for passive voice, past tense, and the required format elements. Partners give one oral suggestion; students make a final revision on the spot before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit introduces report writing in the context of a school science event, grounding the form in the chapter's science theme. A common difficulty is slipping back into active voice and first person; the model sentence on the board serves as a quick reference throughout drafting. The report begins and ends within this unit — planning, drafting, peer response, and revision all occur here so the piece is complete.

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Words, Suffixes, Acronyms, and Active–Passive Voice

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.240): match six sentences to the correct word from the given box.
Let us learn (p.240): add correct suffix (-ship, -ment, -hood) to eight root words.
Let us learn (p.242): complete the malaria vaccine news report using passive forms of six verbs.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.239): complete the antonym crossword puzzle independently at home.

time_bands.activity: Students work individually on the vocabulary matching task (p.240) — substituting underlined phrases with the correct word from the box (physicist, peers, luminaries, barriers, pioneers, persistence). Pairs compare answers and the teacher leads a quick whole-class check.

Teacher draws attention to the words 'professorship', 'mentorship', 'leadership' from the text and models how the suffix '-ship' works. Students then add the correct suffix (-ship, -ment, or -hood) to the eight root words (p.240) and share answers.

Teacher presents the active–passive contrast using the sentence from the text about pioneers (p.242). Students complete the malaria vaccine news report passage by filling in the passive forms of the six verbs provided, working individually then checking in pairs.
Quick whole-class review of the passive-form answers; teacher highlights the pattern of 'was/were + past participle' using two or three student responses written on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is dedicated to vocabulary and grammar, treating word-building, contextual meaning, and passive voice as interconnected strands drawn from the chapter's language. Students often confuse '-ment' and '-ship' suffixes; ground every example in a word from the profile text where possible. The antonym crossword (p.239) is suited to independent home practice since it consolidates vocabulary encountered in the reading.

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Chandrayaan Passive Voice and Women Pioneers Beyond the Text

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.243): choose correct passive-voice options to complete the Chandrayaan passage.
Let us explore (p.249): read about and discuss women pioneers from different fields in India.

time_bands.activity: Students read the Chandrayaan landing instructions (p.243) and individually select the correct passive-voice option for each of the five blanks. Teacher then leads a whole-class check, writing each correct form on the board and explaining why it is the right tense and voice.

Teacher introduces the 'Let us explore' section on women pioneers from different fields (p.249), briefly describing two or three figures not yet mentioned in the profile — drawing a line from Bibha Chowdhuri's era to contemporary scientists.

In small groups, students discuss one woman pioneer each has heard of from any field — science, mathematics, medicine, technology — and agree on two qualities that mark her contribution as pioneering. Each group shares one name and two qualities with the class.

Teacher closes with a brief observation connecting the chapter's profile of Bibha Chowdhuri to the women pioneers students have just discussed, noting the thread of persistence and barrier-breaking across fields.

periods.teacher_notes: Having practised passive voice with the malaria-vaccine passage during the vocabulary-grammar unit, students now apply the same grammatical understanding to the Chandrayaan passage — a context that connects directly to the chapter's celebration of India's space science achievements. The beyond-text discussion deliberately broadens the chapter's scope beyond Bibha to other domains; if students struggle to name pioneers beyond the textbook, prompt them with one example from medicine or mathematics. Tasks on the Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar (p.250) and the AR/VR app (p.249) may serve as independent home reading for interested students.

periods.section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Science, Legacy, and the Beam of Light

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.239): discuss how the renaming of a star as 'Bibha' is both literal and symbolic recognition.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with the question: 'Across this chapter, we have read about cosmic rays, pi-mesons, Chandrayaan, and AI — what single thread connects all of them?' Students call out responses; the teacher maps them on the board under the heading 'Science as Service to Humanity.'

Students work in pairs to discuss the question: 'How does the renaming of the star HD 86081 as "Bibha" serve as both a literal and symbolic recognition of her contributions?' (p.239). Each pair prepares one sentence for each dimension — literal and symbolic.

Pairs share their sentences in a whole-class roundtable. Teacher synthesises the responses into a connected argument: Bibha as a beam of light — the name, the star, the metaphor, and the women of ISRO who follow her — drawing on the profile's concluding paragraphs (p.239–241).

Students write two to three sentences in their notebooks in response to the closing question: 'What does Bibha Chowdhuri's story tell us about what it takes to leave a lasting mark on science?' The teacher invites two or three volunteers to read their responses aloud as the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws together the informational profile of Bibha Chowdhuri, the language work on passive voice and word-building, the panel discussion on technology's impact, and the beyond-text discussion on women pioneers — connecting these strands through the chapter's central metaphor of light. A common difficulty at synthesis stage is students summarising events rather than articulating the chapter's argument; guide them toward the idea that Bibha's legacy is not just historical but a live force shaping Indian science today. This unit assumes students have engaged with the section's content but makes no assumptions about which specific activities, discussions, or pieces of writing they have done.

items.source_section_title: Bibha Chowdhuri — The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science
items.source_lo: Student identifies and interprets key information, infers authorial intent, and evaluates perspective using an informational profile as the vehicle.

items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about Bibha Chowdhuri's life and career. Write True or False for each, and give a one-sentence reason drawn from her profile.
1. Bibha Chowdhuri conducted her doctoral research on cosmic rays under Patrick M.S. Blackett at the University of Manchester.
2. Erwin Schrödinger nominated Bibha Chowdhuri for the Nobel Prize in 1960.
3. She became the first woman faculty member at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, selected by Homi J. Bhabha.
4. The International Astronomical Union renamed a star in the constellation Leo as 'Bibha' in recognition of her legacy.

options.text: Bibha Chowdhuri conducted her doctoral research on cosmic rays under Patrick M.S. Blackett at the University of Manchester.
Erwin Schrödinger nominated Bibha Chowdhuri for the Nobel Prize in 1960.
She became the first woman faculty member at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, selected by Homi J. Bhabha.
The International Astronomical Union renamed a star in the constellation Leo as 'Bibha' in recognition of her legacy.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — She moved to Manchester in 1945 and worked under Blackett on cosmic rays for her Ph.D. 2. False — Schrödinger nominated her in 1950, not 1960. 3. True — Homi J. Bhabha personally selected her as the first woman faculty member at TIFR upon her return to India in 1949. 4. True — The IAU renamed star HD 86081 in the constellation Leo as 'Bibha' in 2019.

Inference that the author argues progress is possible but built on earlier sacrifice.

items.item_stem: After listening to the Tech Talks podcast (p.251–252), choose the correct answer for the following question. According to the podcast, how did AI contribute during the global pandemic?

options.label: A
options.text: AI developed and distributed vaccines independently without human oversight.

options.label: B
options.text: AI helped speed up the discovery of new medicines for the pandemic.

options.label: C
options.text: AI replaced doctors in hospitals to manage the increased patient load.

options.label: D
options.text: AI robots monitored the behaviour of patients in hospitals around the world.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests confusion between AI monitoring tools and the podcast's specific claim about medicine discovery.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Overstates AI autonomy; the podcast emphasises AI as an aid, not an independent actor.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a claim not made in the podcast; reflects a common misconception about AI replacing human professionals.

items.item_stem: The host of Tech Talks (p.251–252) closes the podcast by saying that AI is 'a powerful force for good but we need to use it responsibly.' Based on any TWO segments of the podcast you listened to, write a short answer explaining what evidence the host provides for AI being beneficial, and suggest one reason why responsible use is still necessary.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The host gives examples such as AI enabling faster diagnoses and personalised treatments in healthcare, and improving the performance of wind turbines and solar panels in renewable energy. Responsible use is necessary because AI, if misused or left unregulated, could produce harm — for example, biased diagnoses or over-reliance that reduces human judgement.

items.item_stem:
The sentence below describes an event from Bibha Chowdhuri's career. Rewrite it in the passive voice, and then explain in one sentence why passive voice is commonly used in formal scientific and journalistic writing.

Original sentence: 'Homi J. Bhabha personally selected Bibha Chowdhuri as the first woman faculty member at TIFR.'

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Passive version: 'Bibha Chowdhuri was personally selected by Homi J. Bhabha as the first woman faculty member at TIFR.' Passive voice is commonly used in formal scientific and journalistic writing because it shifts focus from the person performing the action to the event or achievement itself, giving the writing an objective tone.

In your response, refer to at least one specific challenge Bibha faced, one achievement of the ISRO women scientists, and what you think still needs to change for women in STEM.

Identifies something that still needs to change, with a brief reason.

items.source_lo: Student makes interdisciplinary connections, identifies pioneering figures across fields, and reflects on the broader social significance of scientific achievement as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Women pioneers from diverse fields in India; connecting Bibha Chowdhuri's legacy to contemporary scientists and ISRO.
items.item_stem: Design a project proposal (in note form) for a school display titled 'Unsung Pioneers: Women Who Changed Indian Science.' Your proposal must name at least three women from different scientific fields (at least one must be from the chapter), describe one key contribution for each, explain how the display will be presented to the school community, and state what you want viewers to take away from it.

expected_elements: Names at least three women scientists, including Bibha Chowdhuri, from different fields.
Gives one distinct, accurate contribution for each scientist named.
Describes a presentation format (poster, panel, oral presentation, digital display).
States a clear takeaway message connecting the pioneers to today's students.
